name: Svan
confidence_why: Tuite 2023 (like his 1997 and 2003 sketches) describes only a historical strong penultimate accent that later weakened and gives no present-day stress rule, and Gudjedjiani & Palmaitis 1986 state outright that Svan accent "has not been investigated as yet" and only "seems to be free", so the two independent first-hand descriptions agree that no synchronic word-stress rule for Svan is established, while Klimov 1999 offers only a family-level Kartvelian pattern that names no language but Laz.

catalog_quote: Tuite 2023 p. 12: "2.4. Prosodic features. Although Svan does not give one the impression of being a stress-timed language like Russian or English, its morphophonemics bespeak the presence, at an early stage of the language's history, of a strong accent, predominantly falling on the penultimate syllable (see §2.5)." p. 14: "Stage I. Early Svan was characterized by a strong penultimate accent, with reduction or loss of antepenultimate and final vowels, as indicated by forms inherited from Proto-Kartvelian, as well as the oldest loanwords from Georgian ... The one exception was the S1/2sg stem of the past-indicative paradigms (aorist and imperfect), in which, as just mentioned, the accent shifts to the antepenultimate or possibly further leftward." ... "Stage II. At some point the strong penultimate accent of Early Svan became weaker." Gudjedjiani & Palmaitis 1986 p. 23: "2.4. Svan accent has not been investigated as yet. It seems to be free as it is especially clear in radical verbs with preverbs unstressed in the 3rd person in aorist and often stressed in the 1st and 2nd persons (Topuria, 1967). As for the pitch accent (i. e. tone or the syllable accent), the problem has not been even set." p. 24: "Since this phenomenon has not been thoroughly examined, we did not dare mark the supposed tones in our dictionary". Tuite 1997/2004 p. 8: "its morphophonemics bespeak the presence, at some stage of the language's history, of a strong, mobile accent."

new_statements.rule_in_words: No opened source gives a synchronic rule for where word stress falls. Tuite (the standard modern description) says present-day Svan does not sound stress-timed and treats accent only diachronically: Early Svan had a strong penultimate accent (with an exception in 1st/2nd-sg past-indicative stems, where it shifted leftward to the antepenult or further), which later weakened; its traces survive as even-syllable vowel reduction, umlaut and vowel-length alternations. Gudjedjiani & Palmaitis (Upper Bal) state that accent is uninvestigated and 'seems to be free' (mobile, morphologically conditioned in verbs: preverb unstressed in 3rd-person aorist, stressed in 1st/2nd persons), and speculate about a pitch accent tied to vowel length without marking it.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Tuite: the S1/2sg stem of the aorist and imperfect had the (early-Svan) accent shifted leftward from the penult; Lent'ex dialect had a different early accentuation pattern (Tuite 1997/2004 §1.4.1). Gudjedjiani & Palmaitis: preverbs unstressed in 3rd-person aorist but often stressed in 1st/2nd persons.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statements are historical/reconstructive (Tuite) or hedged and unverified (G&P, Upper Bal). Phrase-level: Tuite 2023 p. 76 notes yes/no-question clitics -a/-mo can carry the accent or leave it on the verb's final syllable, -ma and -(j)ā always attract it; Tuite 2023 p. 76 also cites Shavreshiani & Saghliani 2013 on intonational marking of subordination in Lower Bal.
new_statements.identity_note: Tuite 2023 covers all five dialects (Upper Bal, Lower Bal, Lent'ex, Lashx, Cholur) under svan1243; the accent statements are pan-Svan and largely diachronic. Gudjedjiani & Palmaitis 1986 describe Upper Svan (Upper Bal dialect, uppe1417? — Glottolog dialect code not verified) and their 'free accent' remark is dialect-specific to Upper Bal. No source describes a fixed stress position for any dialect.

tone.quote: Svan is likely to be a stress-window language, too, though the facts are not entirely clear. Stress in Svan usually targets the final or penultimate syllable. There might be a tendency for stress to stabilize on the penult (Zhghenti 1949: 100), but stress placement interacts with other processes, such as umlaut, vowel length and vowel reduction ... Long vowels often carry stress: máːre ‘man’ vs. maré ‘but’ (Zhghenti 1949: 97). ... A number of suffixes ... are pronounced as long and viewed as stressed ... Some of these suffixes are also marked by noticeable tonal movement, especially in the Lashkh and Upper Bal dialects (Zhghenti 1949: 101; Zhghenti 1960: 101).
